title: Maine Coon Colors and Patterns: A Guide to Coat Terms
seoTitle: Maine Coon Colors and Patterns: Coat Terms Explained
description: Understand Maine Coon colors and patterns, from tabby to smoke. Learn how to read coat names, compare registry terms and spot the limits of photographs.
html:
You find a kitten you like, then read the breeder’s description: “blue silver classic tabby with white.” The photograph shows a fluffy gray cat. Why does one coat need so many names?

Each word describes a different part of its appearance. Some refer to color, others to markings or the way color sits along the hairs. Once you separate those details, the names become much easier to follow.

This guide explains the main terms you’ll meet while looking at Maine Coon photographs, breeder listings and registration documents. It can help you understand a description, although a photograph alone won’t confirm a cat’s pedigree or exact registered color.

Start with color and pattern

Think of the coat description in two parts: the color you see and the way it appears across the cat.

For example, “tabby” describes markings. It isn’t another name for Maine Coon, and it isn’t one particular color. A coat description can combine a color term with a pattern term, then add details such as white markings.

In the example above, you can read the name piece by piece:

  • Blue: the gray-looking color term.
  • Silver: the pale background beneath the darker markings.
  • Classic tabby: the broad, swirling pattern.
  • With white: separate white areas on the coat.

You don’t have to memorize a long list of combinations. Start by asking which words describe color, which describe markings, and whether the name includes another feature.

The coat terms you’re most likely to encounter

The Cat Fanciers’ Association’s Maine Coon standard describes solid colors, tabby patterns, smoke and other coat groups. Here’s a short reading guide rather than an exhaustive show-class list.

TermWhat it describesUseful distinction
SolidA coat described as one colorCompare the individual color description before assigning a label.
TabbyMarkings across the coatClassic, mackerel and ticked describe different patterns.
Silver tabbyDarker tabby markings over a pale groundKeep the visible markings separate from the word “silver.”
SmokePale undercoat beneath deeply colored hair tipsIt can look darker when the cat is still.
TortoiseshellA combination of black and red color areasBlue-cream is another combination described in the standard.
With whiteWhite areas added to a coat descriptionThis can accompany several underlying colors or patterns.

Different coat groups at a glance

These photographs illustrate white, red tabby with white, and tortoiseshell descriptions supplied by their sources. They are examples of appearance, not independent pedigree verification or a complete identification chart.

Smoke is an easy term to misunderstand from a single picture. The pale undercoat may become clearer when the cat moves or the fur parts. A dark portrait therefore gives you less information than a photograph that shows the relevant coat detail.

For tabbies, a side view is particularly useful. It lets you see body markings that a close-up of the face leaves out.

Why a coat can have more than one description

Some differences are simply about everyday language versus registry language. Other differences come from how coat features combine.

The UC Davis Veterinary Genetics Laboratory explains that several genes influence feline coat appearance, including those involved in agouti patterning and dilution. There isn’t one gene that supplies the whole coat name.

For a pet owner, the practical takeaway is modest: one visible feature doesn’t answer every question about the coat. You can describe what a photograph shows without pretending it reveals the cat’s complete genetic makeup.

If a breeder uses an unfamiliar term, ask them to explain it in ordinary words and show where that feature appears on the kitten. That conversation is usually more helpful than trying to match the kitten to the nearest search-result photograph.

Does every registry use the same rules?

No. A coat pattern being described in one standard does not mean the same showing rules apply everywhere.

CFA includes classic, mackerel and ticked tabby in its Maine Coon standard. The Maine Coon section of GCCF’s May 2025 Standard of Points lists classic and mackerel tabby. The Maine Coon Cat Club’s gallery also notes that ticked and spotted Maine Coons cannot be shown in GCCF.

If you plan to show your cat, check the rules of the actual registry involved. If you’re choosing a companion, don’t mistake a difference in show eligibility for a judgment about whether that cat deserves a good home.

A simple way to read a breeder’s listing

Before deciding that a kitten’s coat has a particular name, work through three questions:

  1. What is the breeder calling it? Ask whether that is an informal description or the recorded registration color.
  2. What can you see? Look for a clear side view, visible markings and any white areas. For smoke, ask for a photograph that shows the undercoat rather than relying on a face portrait.
  3. What remains uncertain? If the picture doesn’t show a feature clearly, leave it uncertain. You don’t need to force a label from an unsuitable photograph.

A photographer’s caption can tell you how they identified their own cat. It isn’t the same as reviewing registration records. We use that distinction in our image captions too.

What the color name won’t tell you

A coat name isn’t a substitute for information about the individual kitten: its background, care, socialization and the breeder’s records.

Treat claims such as “the rarest color” or a premium justified only by a dramatic coat as questions to investigate. This guide does not rank colors by rarity or establish what any kitten should cost.

Once the coat terminology makes sense, return to the things you’ll manage at home. Our Maine Coon grooming guide covers caring for the coat, while the size and growth guide helps you think about the space your cat will need.

Common questions

Is tabby a breed?

No. It describes a coat pattern. Calling a cat tabby does not establish Maine Coon ancestry.

Are smoke and silver tabby the same?

They describe different appearances. Smoke refers to the pale undercoat beneath colored tips; silver tabby includes visible tabby markings over a pale ground. A poorly lit portrait may not show enough detail to distinguish them.

How many Maine Coon colors are there?

For understanding your cat’s coat, a single headline number is less useful than knowing which registry and combinations the list covers. Check the named standard, then read the color and pattern terms separately.

  • Black smoke comparison

title: Tabby Maine Coons: Classic, Mackerel and Ticked Patterns
seoTitle: Tabby Maine Coons: Classic, Mackerel and Ticked Patterns
description: Compare classic, mackerel and ticked tabby Maine Coons. Learn which markings to look for, how registry rules differ and what a photograph cannot confirm.
html:
Two cats can both be described as tabby Maine Coons and still have noticeably different markings. One has broad swirls along its sides. Another has narrow stripes. A third has a more finely textured body coat, with clearer markings around its face and legs.

Tabby describes the markings on the coat. Names such as classic, mackerel and ticked describe how those markings look.

If you’re trying to understand a breeder’s description or identify the markings in a photograph, start with the side of the cat. A face portrait can be lovely, but it often leaves out the detail you need.

Tabby describes markings, not a separate breed

A tabby Maine Coon is a Maine Coon described as having tabby markings. The pattern name alone does not establish the breed.

That distinction matters when you see an unfamiliar long-haired cat. You can describe visible swirls or stripes without deciding that it must be a Maine Coon. Breed background and a coat description are separate questions.

Color is another part of the name. For example, “brown classic tabby” combines a color description with a pattern description. Adding “with white” gives another detail about the coat; it does not replace the underlying pattern.

Our colors-and-patterns overview explains how those parts fit together. Here, the focus is narrower: understanding the markings themselves.

Classic, mackerel and ticked: what to look for

The Cat Fanciers’ Association’s Maine Coon standard describes all three patterns. The table below turns the main visual differences into a practical starting point. It is not a show judging checklist.

PatternMain feature to look forPhotograph that helps
ClassicBroad markings, including substantial rings or blotches on the sidesA clear side view showing most of the body
MackerelNarrower markings around the bodyA side view where the flank is visible rather than hidden by a pose
TickedA finely ticked body coat without obvious body stripes or blotches; markings can remain on the face and legsBoth a whole-body view and a closer view of the coat

The photograph needs to show the feature you’re comparing. If a cat is curled up, its flank may be hidden. If the image shows only the head and chest, it cannot settle a question about side markings.

Classic tabby: look for the broader shapes

For a classic pattern, look beyond a single dark stripe. Notice how the larger markings are arranged across the side of the body.

Our selected classic-tabby photograph shows the cat standing sideways, so the broad markings are visible. The source labels it as a classic-tabby Maine Coon. That makes it a useful example of the appearance being discussed, although we have not reviewed that individual cat’s pedigree documents.

Mackerel tabby: look for narrower markings

For mackerel, compare the narrower body markings with the broader shapes in a classic example. A side photograph is more useful for this than a close-up of the face.

Don’t assume a photograph demonstrates the pattern just because its caption says “mackerel.” The label and the visible evidence do different jobs. A correctly labelled cat may be photographed in a position that hides the very markings the reader needs to see.

Ticked tabby: the body can look less obviously patterned

Ticked is the pattern most likely to confuse someone expecting every tabby to have large body stripes. The distinction concerns the appearance of the body coat, while markings may still show elsewhere.

The labelled schematic above illustrates this distinction. It shows the pattern concept rather than a photograph of an individual cat.

Does the forehead M identify a Maine Coon?

No. It is not a breed certificate.

CFA’s descriptions of classic and mackerel patterns include forehead markings resembling an M. That tells you something about a pattern description; it does not demonstrate an individual cat’s ancestry.

If the question is “What markings can I see?”, examine the coat. If the question is “What is this cat’s documented breed background?”, ask about its records. Trying to answer both from one facial feature creates unnecessary confusion.

Why different guides disagree about accepted patterns

Check which registry a guide is discussing before treating its list as universal.

CFA includes ticked tabby in its Maine Coon standard. The Maine Coon section of GCCF’s May 2025 Standard of Points lists classic and mackerel tabby. The Maine Coon Cat Club’s gallery explicitly notes that ticked and spotted Maine Coons cannot be shown in GCCF.

For anyone planning to show a cat, the relevant registry’s current rules matter. A general list of cat patterns cannot answer that showing question on its own.

For a reader simply learning coat terminology, the useful habit is to keep the pattern description and the registry’s eligibility rules separate.

A better way to compare a kitten’s photographs

You don’t need dozens of pictures. You need pictures that show the right details.

  1. Read the full description. Note the color, pattern and any “with white” wording rather than focusing on one word.
  2. Ask for a side view. Check whether the body markings are visible. If the cat’s position hides them, leave that part uncertain.
  3. Use the caption as a source label. A breeder or photographer’s identification provides context, but it should not be confused with an independent review of registration records.
  4. Ask what the records say. If a registered color or show eligibility matters to you, confirm it with the breeder and the named registry.

A helpful question is: “Could you show me where the classic or mackerel markings are visible in this photo?” It invites an explanation instead of turning the discussion into a guessing game.

Keep coat questions separate from care questions

This article compares appearances. It does not use a pattern name to predict a cat’s personality, health or adult size.

For practical care, use the individual cat’s needs and the appropriate advice. Our grooming guide covers managing the coat, and our size and growth guide covers the measurements that matter when planning space and equipment.

Common questions

Is classic tabby another name for brown tabby?

No. “Classic” describes the pattern, while “brown” describes a color. Read both parts of the coat name rather than using them interchangeably.

Can a ticked tabby have facial markings?

Yes. CFA’s description includes markings on the face and legs, even though the body lacks obvious stripes or blotches. The whole coat matters when comparing patterns.

Can I confirm the pattern from one photo?

Sometimes a suitable image makes the visible markings easy to describe. Other images leave important details hidden. State what you can see, and ask for another view when necessary.

Related coat guides

title: Black Smoke Maine Coons: Smoke vs Solid Black and Silver Tabby
seoTitle: Black Smoke Maine Coons: Smoke, Black and Silver Tabby
description: Compare black smoke Maine Coons with solid black and silver tabby. Learn which coat details to look for and what to ask when photographs leave doubts.
html:
A cat looks almost black in one photograph, then much lighter around the neck in another. The breeder calls it black smoke. Is that a different color, a trick of the lighting, or simply a black cat with a pale ruff?

The useful distinction is in the coat itself. Black smoke describes a pale undercoat beneath deeply colored hair tips. A portrait may show the overall appearance, but it often leaves that detail hidden.

If you’re comparing kittens or trying to understand a coat description, start with what the name means. Then ask whether the photographs actually show the feature you’re looking for.

What does black smoke mean?

The Cat Fanciers’ Association’s Maine Coon standard describes black smoke as a white undercoat beneath deeply black-tipped fur. It also notes that the cat may appear black at rest, with the pale undercoat becoming more apparent in motion or when the fur is parted.

That explains why one full-body photograph may be more helpful than another. A photo of the cat sitting still can show its dark outer coat without clearly revealing the pale base of the hairs.

For a reader learning the term, the important point is the contrast between the underlying coat and the darker tips. There is no need to assign an exact percentage of black and white to every hair.

Black smoke, solid black and silver tabby compared

These names describe different coat appearances. A dark photograph is not enough to make them interchangeable.

Coat descriptionMain distinctionDetail worth looking for
Solid blackCFA describes the black color as extending from the roots to the tips, without a smoke undercoatA clear view of the coat, not just its dark silhouette
Black smokePale undercoat beneath deeply black-tipped hairsA view that actually reveals the underlying fur
Silver tabbyDark tabby markings over a pale groundVisible body markings as well as the lighter background

The comparison gives you a way to read a description. It does not turn a distant or poorly lit photograph into a reliable identification tool.

If the image leaves the relevant detail hidden, the sensible answer is that you need another view.

Why the photograph may not settle the question

Imagine two photos of the same cat. In the first, the cat faces the camera and most of its body is out of frame. In the second, you can see its side and more of the coat.

The second image gives you more information about body markings. Neither necessarily gives you a close view of the hair roots.

Before relying on a picture, ask what it shows:

  • Can you see the whole body or only the face?
  • Are any tabby markings visible along the sides?
  • Does the photograph reveal the underlying fur, or only the outer coat?
  • Is the color description supplied by the owner or breeder, and is it also the recorded registration color?

These questions help you separate a useful observation from a guess. They are especially helpful when a listing contains several attractive portraits but no photograph of the detail being discussed.

Is a pale neck ruff enough to identify black smoke?

It can be part of the appearance described in the standard, but don’t use one pale area as the whole test.

Our selected photograph is labelled as a young black-smoke Maine Coon by its photographer. It shows a dark cat with a lighter ruff. We can use it as a labelled example of overall appearance, while being clear that the picture does not show parted hair roots and we have not reviewed that cat’s pedigree documents.

That distinction also applies to photographs you find elsewhere. A source caption tells you how the owner or photographer identified the cat. It should not be presented as independent verification of every feature in the image.

What about faint stripes on a dark coat?

Faint markings can make a photograph harder to interpret. Avoid jumping from those markings to a new coat label.

The UC Davis Veterinary Genetics Laboratory’s feline coat-color guide notes that tabby patterns can be difficult to identify in non-agouti cats. A few visible lines in a photograph therefore do not, by themselves, settle the cat’s registered color or establish a separate “smoke tabby” classification.

If the label matters, ask the breeder what is recorded and which registry they use. For a pet owner simply learning the terminology, it is enough to acknowledge that the photograph leaves the answer uncertain.

Questions to ask when viewing a kitten

You can keep the conversation simple:

  1. “What is the full coat description?” Check whether “black smoke” is being used informally or matches the registration description.
  2. “Could you show me the coat detail that supports that description?” Ask for a suitable photograph rather than another face portrait.
  3. “Which registry is the kitten registered with?” Use that registry’s terminology when discussing records or showing eligibility.
  4. “What can you tell me about this individual kitten?” Give its background, socialization and care the attention they deserve alongside appearance.

A helpful breeder should be able to explain the label in ordinary words. You should not have to make a purchase decision from a dramatic photograph and an unexplained color name.

Be careful with rarity and price claims

“Rare black smoke” can sound persuasive in a listing. Before treating it as evidence, ask what the claim is based on.

This guide does not rank Maine Coon colors by rarity. We have not gathered a representative color-frequency dataset, and a few listings would not establish one.

The same applies to price. A breeder’s asking price tells you about that offer. It does not establish a standard US price for every black-smoke kitten or prove that the coat alone justifies a premium.

If you like this appearance, that is a perfectly understandable preference. Keep it alongside the other information you need about the kitten rather than letting the color label carry the whole decision.

Caring for the coat you have

The comparison here explains coat terminology. It is not a reason to invent a special feeding routine or promise a particular personality for a black-smoke cat.

For day-to-day coat care, our Maine Coon grooming guide covers the practical routine. Our care guide covers the wider responsibilities of living with a Maine Coon.

Common questions

Is black smoke the same as solid black?

No. The pale undercoat is the distinction in the black-smoke description. A cat may still look very dark when the outer coat hides that detail.

Is black smoke the same as silver tabby?

No. Silver tabby includes visible tabby markings over a pale ground. Black smoke describes a pale undercoat beneath dark tips. Look for the features relevant to each name rather than relying on the word “silver.”

Will a kitten look exactly like an adult photo?

An adult photo can explain a coat term, but it is not a promise about a particular kitten’s future appearance. Ask the breeder about the kitten and avoid treating a reference image as a forecast.

Does black smoke prove that a cat is a Maine Coon?

No. A coat description does not establish an individual cat’s breed background. Ask about its records if pedigree is important to you.
